newsitem.title: UK: BOE's George unsure over regulatory timing.
newsitem.headline: BOE's George unsure over regulatory timing.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday said the central bank was not confident the time was ripe for a single, all-encompassing financial regulator for Britain's financial industry as announced on Tuesday by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.
George told a news conference it had long been clear that changes in the financial markets were causing traditional distinctions between banks and other financial institutions to become blurred.
He said that continuing process would require a single regulator at some point, "But we're not confident that point has been reached now."
George said he did not disagree with the broad principle of a single regulator and that the structure made good sense.
"It's a world we're moving towards, even if we're not there yet," he said, adding: "But the implementation is going to be hugely difficult."
Banks were still special "in a systemic sense", providing liquidity to both depositors and borrowers.

Brown announced on Tuesday that the current Securities and Investments Board (SIB) would be enlarged and strengthened and take over from the Bank the role of supervising the banking industry, under the chairmanship of current BOE deputy governor Howard Davies.

George added that the Bank of England could not be shut out of the regulatory process, and its continuing responsibility for the stability of the financial system would mean close co-operation with the new "mega-regulator".
The Bank has had formal responsibility for regulating the banking industry since 1979 and had previously done so on a more informal basis.
George admitted surprise over the timing of the announcement, saying he had only been told on Monday, but said he had not seriously considered resigning.
Asked if the changes had caused him to consider resignation, he replied: "All sorts of things go through your mind, but frankly not seriously."
He said the fact that Brown had not consulted him about his plans to transfer supervisory responsibility should not be exaggerated, and the policy shift had been well signalled.
"You shouldn't make too much of the lack of consultation," he said. "The surprise was in the timing."
Later, George said that further consultation would have meant an unnecessary delay.

In recent years, banks have started to offer a wider range of services including insurance, pensions and other investment products. Some have moved into the area of investment banking, offering merger advice as well as trading in securities.
George said it was crucial that the regulatory regime must not be restrictive while offering safeguards to depositors and investors.

"It's intrinsic that you have a balance to strike between the innovation and vigour of the markets and the needs of the depositors on the other hand," he said. "Maintaining that balance is at the heart of the regulatory system."
George said he expected Davies to be aware of the dangers of bureaucracy and too much "form-filling and box-ticking."

While the details of how the new SIB will tackle its banking role are far from settled, George made it clear that the new department will be initially staffed by Bank of England people and that its recent measures to bolster supervision of banking will go ahead.
